newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan president sacks Bhutto, names caretaker.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan president sacks Bhutto, names caretaker.

text.p: Pakistani President Farooq Leghari sacked Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto on Tuesday , accusing her government of corruption and nepotism.
Soldiers in the Punjab provincial capital of Lahore detained her husband Asif Ali Zardari, along with Punjab governor Raja Saroop Khan, witnesses said.
It was the second time Bhutto has been sacked.
Army troops moved into the capital Islamabad in the early hours to guard key installations, but kept off the streets, which remained calm. Schools and businesses opened as usual.
Mobile telephone services were disconnected overnight. Home telephones of Bhutto's cabinet ministers were out of service.
Troops also took control of important locations, including international airports, in other cities, witnesses said.
The official news agency APP said the president had ordered general elections for February 3.

Leghari, once a Bhutto loyalist, issued a proclamation dismissing her three-year-old government, which he accused of fostering corruption, undermining the judiciary and failing to stop extra-judicial killings in Karachi and elsewhere.

"Corruption, nepotism and violation of rules in the administration of the affairs of the Government... has become so extensive and widespread that the orderly functioning of Government in accordance of the provisions of the Constitution and the law has become impossible and in some cases, national security has been endangered.
"Public faith in the integrity and honesty of the Government has disappeared," he said.

Bhutto has been in power since general elections in October 1993, her second spell as prime minister after then president Ghulam Ishaq Khan sacked her for similar reasons after 20 months' rule in 1990.
The president has constitutional powers to dismiss elected governments and dissolve parliament's lower house.

Bhutto's spokesman Farhatullah Babar said she was at her official residence in Islamabad, but was not taking calls. He said she had received a letter from Leghari soon after 1.30 a.m. (2130 GMT Monday).
Leghari named former parliament speaker Meraj Khalid, 80, to take charge of an interim government until National Assembly (lower house) elections.
"Our first priority will be to hold free, fair and impartial elections," Khalid told reporters at his home, shortly before leaving for the presidential palace.
Khalid, rector of the International Islamic University in Islamabad, said free and fair elections could not be held unless the election commission was "powerful and independent".
Leghari said Bhutto's government had taken "no meaningful steps" to stop extrajudicial killings he said had cost the lives of thousands of people in Karachi and elsewhere.
Bhutto, he said, had insinuated that the presidency and other state agencies were involved in a conspiracy to kill her brother Murtaza Bhutto, shot dead by police in September.
Bhutto had "ridiculed" a Supreme Court judgment in March on the appointment of judges and delayed its implementation.

Her cabinet had tried to "destroy the independence of the judiciary" by introducing a bill in parliament, without informing the president, which would allow a Supreme Court or High court judge to be sent on forced leave on a motion supported by 15 percent of the National Assembly.
Leghari said Bhutto's government had "deliberately violated on a massive scale the fundamental right to privacy" through "illegal phone-tapping and eavesdropping techniques".
Her government had been beset by mounting political and economic crises, but she had sworn to complete her five-year term until scheduled elections in October 1998.

The government had been close to completing negotiations with the International Monetary Fund on reactivating a stalled $600 million standby loan following last month's devaluation of the rupee and an emergency economic rescue package.
An IMF official said on Tuesday that a visiting IMF mission's talks would continue despite Bhutto's dismissal.
